title: Liberty Proclaimed and Revoked
summary: As Babylon's army closes in on Jerusalem and the last fortified towns, Jeremiah tells Zedekiah that the city will burn and he will be taken to Babylon, though he will die in peace. During the siege Zedekiah leads the people in a solemn covenant to free their Hebrew slaves, but when the Babylonian army withdraws for a time, the owners take their slaves back. The LORD answers with bitter irony: since they would not proclaim liberty, he proclaims liberty for them, liberty to fall by sword, plague, and famine, and the Babylonians will return.
story: After the promises of chapters 30 to 33, the book returns to the siege and to the question of whether Judah will obey. The chapter pairs two scenes. The first repeats the verdict on Zedekiah and his city already given in 21:1-10 and 32:3-5. The second shows the people's heart in action: in danger they make a costly act of obedience, and as soon as the danger seems to pass they undo it. It is a case study of the shallow repentance that has marked the nation throughout the book, and it stands in deliberate contrast with the faithful Rechabites of chapter 35.
historical:
The chapter belongs to the siege of Jerusalem, which began in Zedekiah's ninth year (about 589 or 588 BC) and ended in 587 or 586 BC. Verse 7 says only Lachish and Azekah still held out among Judah's fortified cities. Lachish was the second city of Judah, about thirty miles southwest of Jerusalem, and Azekah lay to its north. Excavations at Lachish uncovered ostraca (letters written in ink on pottery pieces) from this very period, known as the Lachish Letters. One of them, written by an officer at an outpost, says that they are watching for the fire signals of Lachish and cannot see Azekah, which many scholars take to mean that Azekah had already fallen.

Verse 21 refers to the Babylonian army's withdrawal from Jerusalem, which 37:5 explains: an Egyptian army under Pharaoh Hophra (44:30) had marched out, and the Babylonians broke off the siege to meet it. It was during this lull that the slave owners changed their minds. The Babylonians soon returned, as Jeremiah said.
cultural:
Israel's law allowed a fellow Israelite who fell into debt to sell himself (or be sold) into service, but he was to be released in the seventh year (Exodus 21:2-6; Deuteronomy 15:12-18). Deuteronomy adds that the freed servant must be sent away with provisions, remembering that Israel had been slaves in Egypt. The word for liberty in verses 8, 15, and 17 is the one used for the Jubilee proclamation in Leviticus 25:10. Verse 14 says this law had long been ignored.

The covenant ceremony described in verses 18 and 19 was a well-known ancient ritual. An animal was cut in two, and the parties walked between the halves, in effect saying: may I be cut apart like this if I break my oath. God himself passes between the pieces in his covenant with Abraham (Genesis 15:9-17). An eighth-century BC Aramaic treaty found at Sefire in Syria contains a similar curse involving a calf cut in two. The spices burned for dead kings (verse 5) were part of an honorable royal funeral, like the fire made for King Asa (2 Chronicles 16:14).
literary: The chapter's two parts are both framed as words to Jeremiah during the siege. Verses 1 to 7 are a short oracle to Zedekiah with a narrative note on the military situation. Verses 8 to 22 tell the story of the release and its reversal, then give God's judgment. That judgment is built on wordplay. The verb shuv (turn, return) describes both the people's repentance in verse 15 and their turning back in verses 11 and 16; they turned and then turned again. The word liberty (deror) is proclaimed by the people, withheld, and then proclaimed by God in a terrible reversal (verse 17). The cut calf of verse 18 becomes the image of what the covenant breakers will suffer. The chapter ends where it began, with the city burned.

outline.t: A word to Zedekiah as the last cities hold out
The covenant of release and its profanation
Liberty to the sword; the calf cut in two

doctrines.note: The people genuinely did right (verse 15) and then reversed it when pressure eased. Repentance that lasts only as long as the crisis is not the turning God seeks.

The law of release protected the poor from permanent bondage and reminded Israel that God had freed them from Egypt. Ignoring it was a failure of justice, not a mere technicality, and God treats it as a covenant breach.
Taking back the slaves profaned God's name (verse 16) because the release had been sworn in his house and before him. Oaths made in God's name bind the one who swears them.

words.note: Deror, liberty or release, the word used for the Jubilee in Leviticus 25:10 and for the proclamation of liberty to captives in Isaiah 61:1. It is related to an Akkadian term for royal decrees of debt release. In verse 17 God turns it into irony: the liberty they denied others becomes liberty for disaster.

Chophshi, free, the status of a released slave. It appears in the law of release (Exodus 21:2; Deuteronomy 15:12) and five times in this chapter, underlining that the covenant was about real people regaining real freedom.

Berit, covenant. The chapter plays God's covenant from the exodus (verse 13) against the people's covenant to free their slaves (verses 8, 15, 18). Breaking the second exposed their contempt for the first.
Egel, calf or young bull. The calf cut in two was the physical sign of the covenant oath. God says the covenant breakers will become like it (verse 18).

christ: The liberty proclaimed and betrayed in this chapter is the language Jesus used to describe his own mission. In the synagogue at Nazareth he read from Isaiah 61, where the servant of the LORD is sent to proclaim liberty to the captives, and he declared that the Scripture had been fulfilled that day (Luke 4:16-21). Isaiah's word for liberty is the same deror used here. Where Judah's leaders proclaimed freedom and took it back, Jesus announced a release that he did not revoke. The cut-covenant ritual also forms part of the background of the New Testament's covenant language: in Genesis 15 God alone passes between the pieces, taking the curse on himself, and many Christian interpreters see that pattern completed at the cross, where Christ bore the curse of the broken covenant (Galatians 3:13). That is a theological connection, not a New Testament comment on this chapter.

hard.q: Jeremiah promised Zedekiah he would die in peace, but 52:10-11 says the Babylonians killed his sons before his eyes, blinded him, and kept him in prison until he died. Was the prophecy wrong?
hard.a: Interpreters answer in different ways. Many read verses 4 and 5 as conditional: the promise of a peaceful death with royal honors belonged to Zedekiah if he surrendered, as Jeremiah later urged him to do (38:17-18), and he did not. Others take it more narrowly: Zedekiah did not die by the sword but by natural causes in captivity, and he may have received mourning rites from the exiles, which is all the verse strictly says. Still others note that the words of verse 3 (captured, taken to Babylon, seeing the king face to face) were fulfilled exactly and that verses 4 and 5 soften without cancelling that verdict. The first reading fits the book's broader pattern of warnings that depend on the hearer's response.

questions: The people freed their slaves under threat and took them back when the threat eased. Where have you made promises to God in a crisis that faded when the crisis passed?
The law of release was grounded in Israel's memory of being slaves in Egypt. How should remembering what God has done for you shape the way you treat people who depend on you?
God treated the broken promise to slaves as a breach of his covenant. What does that say about how seriously God takes justice for the vulnerable?
